newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr sticks to US$ as yen storms market.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr sticks to US$ as yen storms market.

text.p: The Australian dollar stuck to familiar ground on its U.S. counterpart Wednesday but went on a whistle stop tour of yen levels not seen in ten-months.

Traders said Tokyo dumped AUD/yen to depths last plumbed in August 1996 after US$/yen slumped below 112.00 in a stop loss rout to 111.00. The pressure spilled over in AUD/US$ for a while, but support around US$0.7585 proved solid once again.

Leading data on the domestic economy merely puzzled in their contradictions with housing finance up strongly but consumer sentiment down for the third month in a row, suggesting Australia was a nation of depressed home buyers.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local currency had settled at US$0.7595/00 having drifted down from a US$0.7628 high overnight and US$0.7610/15 late here Tuesday.
On the crosses it fled to 84.20/30 yen from an early 85.10/20 and 85.95/05 late Tuesday.
It was hot on the heels of the U.S. dollar which slid below 111.00 yen for the first time since November 1996 having lost more than a yen since the opening.
Traders attributed much of the fall to panic stop loss selling and said it reflected underlying unease about Japan's trade surplus, which was growing again after months of decline.

Data for April out this morning showed Japan's current account surplus had ballooned by 92.7 percent on the same month last year to 1.09 trillion yen. That implied an increased net demand for yen for trade purposes and also stirred concerns of renewed trade friction between Japan and the U.S.
Those worries were stoked by comments from U.S. deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers that Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.
Analysts said the market suspected Japan was keen to see a higher yen short term to deflect any trade criticism that might be levelled at the forthcoming G7 meeting in Denver.

The latest slide in AUD/yen brought the local currency's losses to more than 15 percent since it peaked at 100.00 yen on May 1. And there was little in the way of chart support to prevent it from plumbing the 82.00 trough touched in early August last year.
The dollar's attraction was further dimmed by persistent speculation the Reserve Bank would ease for a fifth time this cycle, a concern today's data were too mixed to alleviate.
Housing finance was healthy enough with a 12.2 percent rise in April being the largest monthly gain since late 1993. Total commitments were at their highest level since July 1994.
Lending for new construction rose 12.1 percent and promised to fuel future growth in the housing and building sectors.
However, while consumers were out buying homes they did not seem to be feeling happy about it.

The June Westpac-Melbourne Institute index of consumer sentiment fell 2.5 points, or 2.4 percent, its third monthly drop in a row. The result confounded expectations the official rate cut of May 23 would have bolstered confidence as, historically, easings tend to do.
Westpac blamed the peverse reading on concerns about unemployment, a timely warning given jobs data are due Thursday.
Median forecasts are for a 15,000 rise in employment following April's 37,100 gain, itself a bounce from back-to-back falls in February and March.
Monthly jobs growth at that level would only be enough to keep the jobless rate stable at 8.7 percent, a level the RBA has often expressed disappointment at.
And market range as low as a 5,000 fall for employment, a result which would have the money market baying for an immediate easing.
In trade weighted terms the dollar finished at 57.3 down from 57.6 late Tuesday. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
